title: Grade 11 Chemistry — Chemical Bonding & States of Matter
description: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure and States of Matter practice questions
subject: chemistry

questions.question: An ionic bond is formed by:
options: Sharing of electrons between two atoms
Transfer of electrons from one atom to another
questions.explanation: Ionic bonds form when one atom transfers electrons to another, creating oppositely charged ions that attract each other. Example: Na⁺Cl⁻ in NaCl.

questions.question: The VSEPR model predicts the shape of a molecule based on:
options: Repulsion between electron pairs around the central atom
questions.explanation: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory: electron pairs arrange themselves to minimise repulsion. This determines molecular geometry (linear, bent, tetrahedral, etc.).

questions.question: Water (H₂O) is a bent molecule with bond angle approximately:
questions.explanation: H₂O has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs. VSEPR predicts bent geometry. Lone pairs compress the bond angle from tetrahedral 109.5° to about 104.5°.

questions.question: A coordinate (dative) bond is formed when:
options: Both atoms share one electron each
One atom provides both electrons of the shared pair
questions.explanation: A dative (coordinate) covalent bond forms when one atom (donor) provides both electrons of the shared pair to another atom (acceptor). Example: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺.

questions.question: The hybridisation of carbon in methane (CH₄) is:
questions.explanation: In CH₄, carbon forms 4 equivalent bonds. One 2s and three 2p orbitals mix to form 4 equivalent sp³ hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally. Bond angle = 109.5°.

questions.question: Hydrogen bonding is strongest in:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding strength depends on electronegativity and size of the atom bonded to H. F is the most electronegative element, making H-F···F-H bonds the strongest.

questions.question: The shape of BF₃ (Boron trifluoride) according to VSEPR theory is:
questions.explanation: BF₃ has 3 bonding pairs and no lone pairs around B. VSEPR predicts trigonal planar geometry with bond angles of 120°. B is sp² hybridised.

questions.question: Electronegativity difference between atoms determines:
options: The polar nature of the bond (ionic or covalent character)
questions.explanation: Large electronegativity difference (> 1.7) → ionic bond. Small difference (< 0.5) → non-polar covalent. Intermediate → polar covalent. Example: HCl is polar covalent.

questions.question: Boyle's law states that at constant temperature, pressure and volume of a gas are:
questions.explanation: Boyle's law: P ∝ 1/V at constant T and n. PV = constant. If pressure doubles, volume halves.

questions.question: Charles' law states that at constant pressure, volume and temperature of a gas are:
questions.explanation: Charles' law: V ∝ T at constant P. V/T = constant. Temperature must be in Kelvin.

questions.question: The ideal gas equation is:
questions.explanation: PV = nRT, where P = pressure, V = volume, n = moles, R = 8.314 J/(mol·K), T = temperature in Kelvin. This combines Boyle's, Charles', and Avogadro's laws.

questions.question: Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour significantly at:
questions.explanation: Real gases deviate most from ideal at high pressure (molecules close together — repulsion matters) and low temperature (molecules slow — intermolecular attractions significant).

questions.question: The kinetic energy of gas molecules is directly proportional to:
questions.explanation: Average kinetic energy of gas molecules = (3/2)kT, where k is Boltzmann's constant and T is temperature in Kelvin. KE is directly proportional to T.

questions.question: Van der Waals equation (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT corrects for:
options: Only the volume of gas molecules
Both finite volume of molecules and intermolecular forces
questions.explanation: Van der Waals equation accounts for: (1) 'nb' corrects for finite volume of molecules; (2) 'an²/V²' corrects for intermolecular attractions. 'a' and 'b' are constants specific to each gas.

questions.question: Surface tension in liquids is due to:
options: Unbalanced intermolecular forces on surface molecules
questions.explanation: Molecules inside a liquid are pulled equally in all directions. Surface molecules experience a net inward pull (unbalanced forces), creating surface tension — a tendency to minimise surface area.
